wine.name: Manso de Velasco Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, from one old vineyard.
wine.sites: The Viñedo del Gobernador Manso de Velasco near Molina in the Curicó Valley, Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1902 on its own roots by the house's account, and bought by the family in 1984 to keep the old vines.
wine.making: Made as a single vineyard wine since its first vintage of 1985, it brought ageing in new oak and then in bottle to the house's Chilean range, by its own account. The house's sheet for 2019 gives eighteen months, partly in French barrels and mostly in large casks of German oak, and later vintages have rested longer in wood, mostly in large casks; it then rests in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackberry and redcurrant with clove and bay leaf, and in some vintages a minty, eucalyptus edge; juicy acidity and a silky start, with tannin that returns on the finish with a fine grain.
wine.ageing: Closed in its first years by the tasting notes read, it wants time in bottle and opens slowly.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The colonial governor who founded the city of Curicó in 1743; the vineyard and the wine carry his name.

records.table: Manso de Velasco is the Cabernet Sauvignon of Miguel Torres Chile, from one Curicó vineyard planted in 1902 on its own roots and named for the governor who founded the city. Cassis and clove over juicy acidity and firm tannin: give it air and a Bordeaux glass.
records.story: The Torres family of the Penedès came to Chile in 1979, when its company founded Miguel Torres Chile in the Curicó Valley: it bought vineyards at Maquehua, San Francisco Norte and Cordillera, with a winery, near the city of Curicó. The house was among the first in Chile to ferment in stainless steel at controlled temperatures, and it was one of the first foreign wine companies to buy land in the country and build a winery there. In 1984 the family bought an old vineyard of Cabernet Sauvignon, planted in 1902 on its own roots by the house's account, to make a wine of one vineyard and to save the vines. The first vintage followed in 1985, and by the house's account it was its first premium wine in Chile and the first of its Chilean wines aged in new oak and then in bottle. The vineyard was renamed for José Antonio Manso de Velasco (about 1688 to 1767), the governor who founded Curicó on 9 October 1743. Miguel Torres Chile is the family's Chilean company, separate from its Spanish wines such as Mas La Plana. Manso de Velasco shows what a Spanish family found in Curicó: old, ungrafted Cabernet, made as a single vineyard wine from the start.

wine.name: Caballo Loco
wine.appellation: A blend of several Chilean valleys
wine.grapes: A blend set anew for each number: Cabernet Sauvignon at the core of many releases, with Carmenère, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Syrah.
wine.sites: Fruit drawn from several valleys and set anew for each number: Maipo Cabernet Sauvignon at the core, Colchagua Carmenère, Curicó Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Malbec, Limarí Syrah in recent numbers, and Maule Grenache and Tannat first in Number 20.
wine.making: Each release is two halves: half new wine of the latest harvests, blended by the house, and half a reserve kept back from the release before, in the manner of a sherry solera. So every number holds a little of the blend of 1994, and the bottle carries a number, never a vintage.
wine.glass: Dark cherry, cassis and espresso with sweet baking spice in recent numbers; the later releases are fresher, with brighter acidity, than the rich, Cabernet led style of the early ones.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink, with old reserve wine already in the blend; older numbers keep for some years in bottle.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant for half an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Caballo Loco is Valdivieso's numbered red: each release is half new wine and half a reserve kept back from the one before, in the manner of a solera, so it carries a number, never a vintage. Dark cherry and cassis; pour it as you would a Bordeaux blend.
records.story: Valdivieso began with bubbles. In 1879, by the house's account, its founder set out to make sparkling wine, and the house traded as Champagne Valdivieso, the first maker of sparkling wine in Chile and in South America as it tells its story. Its still wines came much later, made at its Lontué winery in the Curicó Valley; the house and other accounts disagree on the decade. In 1994 Valdivieso launched Caballo Loco, a red with no vintage. Number One blended Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Pinot Noir of the 1992, 1993 and 1994 harvests, and its maker bottled half and kept half back. That reserve became a kind of solera: every release since has been half the reserve and half new wine, so Number 20, the anniversary release, holds a share of wine from the blend of 1994. The name, crazy horse, was the nickname of a winemaker of the house. Over the years the blend moved from a rich red led by Cabernet towards a fresher one drawn from many valleys, and a white Caballo Loco and single valley Grand Cru wines joined it. For a sommelier it is the rare Chilean red that is sold by number.

wine.name: País Salvaje
wine.grapes: País alone, from very old vines that grow wild.
wine.sites: Wild País vines that seeded themselves among the trees of a creek beside the Mingre vineyard, in the dry secano interior of the Maule about 45 kilometres from the Pacific, on old granitic soils.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand from the wild vines. Part of the fruit, about a third by the importer's sheets, goes through carbonic maceration; the wine ferments with its own yeasts, sees no oak at any stage and is bottled unfiltered.
wine.glass: Red cherry and wild strawberry with a floral lift, forest herbs, pepper and a touch of turned earth; lean and fresh, with grippy, rustic tannin and a savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk young and fresh, within a few years of the vintage.
wine.serve: 13 to 14 degrees Celsius, a little cool; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: Spanish for wild: the vines grow untrained, climbing up into the trees.
The grape the Spanish brought to Chile, the Listán Prieto of the Canaries and the Mission of California.
The name the house's wines carried on earlier labels; recent ones read Bouchon.

records.table: País Salvaje is Bouchon's wild wine: País from vines that seeded themselves and climb into the trees beside the family's Mingre vineyard in the Maule secano. Part carbonic, native yeast and no oak give red cherry and forest herbs; pour it a little cool.
records.story: The Bouchon family is French by origin. Its founder in Chile, a winemaker from Bordeaux and the great grandfather of the generation that runs the house, crossed to Chile in the late nineteenth century to work as a winemaker; accounts of the year differ. A later generation studied wine in Bordeaux and came home to make wine of its own at Mingre, in the dry secano interior of the Maule, where the family farms old vines and sets out to rescue the heritage grapes of southern Chile: País, Semillon, Carignan and Cinsault. In a creek beside the vineyard, País had seeded itself and grown wild among the trees, untouched and unpruned. The family picked it and made País Salvaje, and in 2015 the wine reached the British press: the Drinks Business first called it Chile's first wild wine, then corrected itself, since Villalobos in Colchagua had made a wild vine Carignan for some years before, since 2008 by the magazine's correction. The Mingre vineyard is farmed organically, by the house's account, and the family, which joined VIGNO after its founding, also makes a Carignan under its rules; the association of Maule Carignan was legally constituted in 2011. País Salvaje is the old grape of the Spanish colonists in its most untamed form.

wine.name: Cru Truquilemu Carignan
wine.grapes: Carignan, the great majority, from an old field blend that also holds Monastrell, País, Malbec and Negramoll; recent releases carry a little Syrah fermented with it.
wine.sites: The old Truquilemu vineyard on the road to Empedrado and the coast, high in the Coastal Range: dry farmed bush vines on granitic soils, worked by hand and horse; the Cru is drawn from a low yielding section.
wine.making: Fermented with its own yeasts in small open fermenters, with gentle punch downs by hand and a share of whole bunches and stems. The wine is then aged slowly over two winters in old barrels, of third use or older, before bottling.
wine.glass: Sour cherry and pomegranate with a touch of caramel and garrigue herbs; taut, juicy acidity carries fine grained tannin to a fresh, mouth watering finish.
wine.ageing: Bright enough to drink on release, its acidity and tannin carry it for years in bottle.
wine.serve: 15 to 16 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's selection from a low yielding section of the old Truquilemu vineyard.
Grown with no irrigation, on the winter rain alone.
Several grapes planted together in one vineyard and picked and fermented together.

records.table: Cru Truquilemu is Garage Wine Co.'s Carignan from old dry farmed bush vines at Truquilemu, on the road to Empedrado in the Maule. Native yeasts, old barrels and two winters of rest give sour cherry and pomegranate over taut, juicy acidity.
records.story: Garage Wine Co. began in 2001 in a garage in Santiago, a hobby of three founders. As the house tells it, after half a dozen vintages sold to family and friends, a Chilean newspaper wrote of that garage wine company, and the name stuck; by the house's account it began to export to Britain and Denmark in 2006. Its turn to the Maule came through its growers: the house saw the farmers who sold it Carignan paid little for the rest of their fruit, so it began to buy small lots from them to experiment, and the Single Ferment series followed. Truquilemu, on the road to Empedrado, is one of those vineyards: an old field blend of bush vines, mostly Carignan, with Monastrell the team grafted on to País roots, and País, Malbec and Negramoll among them, farmed by hand and horse. After the earthquake of 2010, a group of Maule producers formed VIGNO, legally constituted in 2011, for old, dry farmed Carignan of the secano, and Garage Wine Co. makes a VIGNO bottling from Truquilemu. The Cru is the vineyard's own selection. To a sommelier it is the Carignan revival told from a smallholder's vineyard.

wine.name: Orzada Carignan
wine.sites: Old head trained Carignan at the Tres Esquinas vineyard in Cauquenes, dry farmed in the Maule secano and more than a hundred years old by the house's account, with fruit from Melozal in Loncomilla on the sheet for 2021.
wine.making: Picked by hand and destemmed without crushing, the whole berries soak cold for four days, ferment with native yeasts in large tanks and macerate for ten days more; malolactic follows of its own accord in tank, by the house's sheet for 2021. The sheet names no barrel.
wine.glass: Blackberry, raspberry and sour cherry with a lift of hibiscus, liquorice and a loamy note; vibrant, with fine but firm tannin and a juicy finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and ready within a few years of the vintage, it holds for several more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: A Spanish sailor's word for sailing up into the wind, the name of the house's varietal range.
From vineyards certified organic by Ecocert, as the house states.

records.table: Orzada Carignan is Odfjell's Maule Carignan, from old dry farmed bush vines at Tres Esquinas in Cauquenes, farmed organically. Bramble fruit, sour cherry and a lift of hibiscus over fine, firm tannin; pour it as a medium bodied red.
records.story: Odfjell is a house of a Norwegian family of shipowners. Its founder came to Chile and fell for the Maipo Valley; accounts differ on when he bought land at Padre Hurtado, at first a fruit farm, and when the first vines went in, in the early 1990s. The gravity flow winery there, designed by one of his sons, an architect, and built in 1997, stands in the Maipo, and the family's first range of wines, launched in 1999, took the name Armador, the ship owner. The house's Carignan began further south. Odfjell bought old Carignan from Cauquenes in the dry secano of the Maule, made its first varietal Carignan in 2001, and that year was reported to have bought land in the Maule whose old vines it had been buying from. The house counts itself among the first to explore Cauquenes and its Carignan. The vineyard, Tres Esquinas, holds head trained, dry farmed Carignan more than a hundred years old, and its fruit went into Orzada, named in the sailor's word for sailing into the wind. Odfjell is a member of VIGNO, the association for old Maule Carignan legally constituted in 2011, with a bottling of its own. Orzada shows the Maule's old Carignan in the hands of a Maipo house.

Orzada is the house's varietal range, with a Cabernet Sauvignon and a Carmenère beside the Carignan; the long aged old vine Carignan is the Vigno.

opts: Tres Esquinas in Cauquenes, in the Maule secano
Padre Hurtado in the Maipo Valley
Ribera del Río Claro in the Lontué
The Casablanca coast near Valparaíso
questions.exp: The Carignan grows at Tres Esquinas in Cauquenes, dry farmed in the Maule secano; Padre Hurtado in the Maipo is where the winery stands.

questions.q: In which trade did the family behind Odfjell Vineyards make its name before it turned to Chilean wine?
opts: Shipping
Banking
Mining
Timber
questions.exp: The founder was a Norwegian shipowner, hence the names Armador, the ship owner, and Orzada, a sailing word; banking plays no part in the house's story.

report: The founding is unsettled: the house says its founder came to Chile in the late 1980s, other accounts that he bought Padre Hurtado in 1982 and planted in 1991, 1992 or 1994, so founded is empty and the story gives the early 1990s; the founder and his sons are living and are not named.
The winery in the Maipo is confirmed by the house (Padre Hurtado); the record teaches the house here for its Cauquenes Carignan, as the plan asks.
The first varietal Carignan of 2001 rests on two secondary accounts; the Maule land bought in 2001 rests on one Wine Spectator report, told as reported.
The end of oak ageing after 2012 rests on one account; the house's sheet for 2021 names tank fermentation and malolactic and no barrel, so the making says by one account.
Biodynamic certification by Demeter rests on one tasting note and is left out; organic certification by Ecocert is the house's own.
The year the winery was designed, 1997, rests on one account and is left out.
Searches spent on this record: 6 of the author's share of 35, with 6 more spent across the group on VIGNO and the governor's dates.

changed: wine.making: the end of oak after 2012, on one account, cut; the 2021 sheet names no barrel.
story: Odfjell's joining VIGNO at its founding in 2011 was not confirmed; now a member, the association legally constituted in 2011.
story: the winery now a gravity flow building of 1997, designed by a son who is an architect, by two accounts.
open: The first plantings at Padre Hurtado (1991, 1992 or 1994) stay unsettled and are told as the early 1990s.
